outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the problem has seen an analytic-case simplification (Guckenheimer, Feb 2024), a 2025 survey restating the Guilfoyle-Klingenberg 2008 proof for C^{3+alpha} surfaces as published, a C^2-case claim by Ando and Umehara (Dec 2025) that was withdrawn after the authors found a gap, and an unrefereed claim by Levent Alpöge (19 Aug 2026) of an explicit C^infinity counterexample with one umbilic, checked per secondary reports with Anthropic's Claude and formalised as draft Lean PRs; the last conflicts with the Guilfoyle-Klingenberg theorems and no independent check was found.
problem_asks: (1) Closed convex surfaces in Euclidean 3-space (the statement says 'convex, closed'; the proof literature says 'strictly convex'). (2) Regularity: twice differentiable, i.e. class C^2; the statement does not restrict to analytic, smooth, or C^{3+alpha} surfaces, so a C^2 surface is in scope. (3) The quantity: umbilic points, where the two principal curvatures coincide. (4) The claim: every such surface admits at least two umbilic points (a universal claim over all such surfaces). Per the sources, 'at least one' follows from topology; the content of the statement is the second umbilic. The statement asks for no index bound and no analogue; index arguments are proof routes, not the question. Nothing in the statement concerns non-Euclidean metrics.

events.what_happened: Hans Ludwig Hamburger published an affirmative answer for real-analytic surfaces in three parts, 'Beweis einer Caratheodoryschen Vermutung' I-III (Ann. Math. and Acta Math., 1940-41), per the Wikipedia article. Hamburger had attributed the conjecture to Carathéodory at a Berlin Mathematical Society session in 1924. The primary papers were not opened.
events.delivers: Real-analytic closed convex surfaces in E^3 have at least two umbilic points, as claimed by Hamburger. Scope: analytic class only.
events.remains: The C^2 class and the smooth non-analytic class, which the statement covers.
events.doubts: Later papers re-examine the analytic chain: Ivanov (2002) 'revisited Hamburger's analytic work'; Klotz and Scherbel found gaps in other analytic proofs (see bol-1944-klotz-1959 and titus-1973-analytic). Whether Hamburger's own argument is regarded as complete was not established from the sources read.
events.direction: Affirms the conjecture for real-analytic surfaces.

sources.why: history of the analytic case, per summarising fetch

events.what_happened: Gerrit Bol proposed a shorter proof for the analytic case, 'Über Nabelpunkte auf einer Eiflache', Math. Z. 49 (1944) 389-410 (Wikipedia gives 1943-44). Tilla Klotz examined it, 'On G. Bol's proof of Carathéodory's conjecture', Commun. Pure Appl. Math. 12(2) (1959) 277-311, and per Wikipedia identified a gap, which one Wikipedia passage says she also corrected. Primary papers not opened.
events.delivers: Bol: a claimed analytic-case proof. Klotz: a gap in it, which Wikipedia also says was corrected. Scope: analytic class only.
events.remains: The C^2 and smooth non-analytic classes; and, if Klotz's correction is not accepted, the analytic class as well.

events.what_happened: Brendan Guilfoyle and Wilhelm Klingenberg, 'Proof of the Caratheodory Conjecture', arXiv:0808.0851 (v1 6 Aug 2008; v2 16 Feb 2012; v3 31 Jul 2013; v4 1 Oct 2024). Main theorem: every closed strictly convex surface in Euclidean 3-space has at least two umbilic points, proved for C^{3+alpha}-smooth surfaces. Argument: reformulate via complex points on a Lagrangian surface in TS^2 (oriented geodesics); a single umbilic would give a totally real hemisphere whose boundary cannot bound a holomorphic disc; construct the disc by mean curvature flow. The v4 text says: 'While the conjecture applies to C2-smooth surfaces, we prove it for C3+alpha-smooth surfaces.' The proof's parts are arXiv:1812.00707, 1812.00710 and 2002.12787 (separate events below).
events.revisions: v2 16 Feb 2012; v3 31 Jul 2013; v4 1 Oct 2024 (current; falls inside the window and is a revision only; the argument is the 2008 one, as far as I could tell from the text read).
events.delivers: Restricted case: C^{3+alpha}-smooth closed strictly convex surfaces have at least two umbilic points (the authors' own statement of their scope). The class is 'strictly convex', whereas the statement says 'convex'.
events.remains: The statement's C^2 class, which the authors say they do not prove; and the non-strictly-convex case, if the statement is read to include it.

events.what_happened: John Guckenheimer, 'Degenerate Umbilic Points of Analytic Surfaces', arXiv:2402.17060 (v1 26 Feb 2024; v2 31 Jan 2025; 15 pages). The abstract gives 'a simpler geometric argument' that the index of an umbilic on an analytic surface cannot be an integer larger than one, and lower bounds on index from degeneracy. It says all (purported) proofs of the Carathéodory conjecture are based on analyses of the index of an umbilic, and that the conjecture's status is controversial (papers claiming proofs followed by work describing deficiencies). The body cites Guilfoyle and Klingenberg once, in a 2006 reference; it does not discuss their 2008 proof.
events.delivers: A simpler argument for the analytic case (index at most one for analytic surfaces), which implies the analytic conjecture since umbilic indices sum to two. Scope: analytic surfaces only.
events.remains: The C^2 and smooth non-analytic classes of the statement.

events.what_happened: Levent Alpöge announced on X (19 Aug 2026) an explicit C^infinity counterexample to the Carathéodory conjecture: a family g_k of functions, of which g_2 is said to be the support function of a smooth strictly convex body with exactly one umbilic point, at the origin, of index 2. The formula (seed f(x+iy) = -1/4 cos 2x + 3/10 cos 2y - 1/32 cos 4y + sin x sin y; g_k(z) = 10^10 + (|z|^2/(1+|z|^2)) exp(-|z|^(-1/4) e^(-|z|^2)) f((100/zbar)^(k/2))) is as reproduced by a summarising fetch of the formalisation's informal-proof page, not checked against the post. The same family is said to disprove the smooth Loewner conjecture (VibeMathed) and to break the Loewner index conjecture (a Chinese press report, 21 Aug 2026). Wikipedia says the counterexample was 'checked with John-Paul Smith and Anthropic's artificial-intelligence system Claude'. The Chinese report says a PDF 'circulated in mathematics circles for a whole week' and has now been 'officially made public', with no link. The formalisation page says 'the circulated writeup mentioned in the post is not public at the time of writing'. The X post returned HTTP 402 and was not read.
events.revisions: No revision of the X post seen. The Chinese report (21 Aug 2026) says a PDF was made public; I did not locate it. Lean formalisations are separate events (alpoge-lean-2026-08-19).
events.delivers: If the construction is right: a C^infinity closed convex surface (a smoothly embedded 2-sphere bounding a strictly convex body) with exactly one umbilic. C^infinity lies inside the statement's twice-differentiable class, so one such example refutes the universal claim as stated. Also claimed: the smooth Loewner conjecture fails.
events.remains: If correct, nothing of the statement remains open for the C^2 class. Not addressed by this claim: the analytic case (Hamburger, Ivanov, Guckenheimer), which VibeMathed says 'remains true'.

I did not carry out this check, and the formula came through a summarising fetch.

disputes.summary: The Alpöge C^infinity counterexample (19 Aug 2026) and the Guilfoyle-Klingenberg theorem for C^{3+alpha} strictly convex surfaces (2008, v4 2024), and their index bound of less than two for C^{3+alpha} (v3 2026), cannot all hold. Neither source has been withdrawn in what I could read. The record does not decide between them.

Role of Claude in the Alpöge result is disputed: Wikipedia and the formalisation docstring say Claude checked the construction with John-Paul Smith; a VibeMathed page records 'AI-assisted' and 'co-developed'; a commenter quotes the author and suggests the example may have been AI-given; a Chinese press report says 'jointly with Claude'. The primary post was not read.

Whether the Alpöge write-up is public: the formalisation page says the circulated writeup 'is not public at the time of writing' (around 21-22 Aug 2026); a Chinese press report of 21 Aug 2026 says it 'has now been officially made public'. No link to a PDF was found.

Regularity class of the 2008 Guilfoyle-Klingenberg result: the abstract and main theorem say C^{3+alpha}; a search snippet says the later version extends it to C^{2+alpha} sections; the v4 text, read through a summarising fetch, says the reformulated version is proven for C^{2+alpha} Lagrangian sections. The statement's class is C^2.
Ghomi-Howard (2011/2012): Wikipedia attributes weak counterexamples (C^1, smooth away from a point, one umbilic) to this paper; the arXiv abstract mentions only the reformulation and weaker forms.
A search-index summary says the 2026 revision of arXiv:1207.5994 'resolves' the Carathéodory conjecture; the v3 abstract states only the C^{3+alpha} index bound and does not mention the conjecture.

Guilfoyle and Klingenberg's 2025 survey says the Carathéodory proof 'has been published by the authors in [14] (see [15] [16] [17])'; the Wikipedia article says that in 2025 they 'claimed three later papers established the conjecture'. The published parts are TAMS 2019, AFST 2020 and GGT 2024; the main article [14] has no journal entry of its own.

summary: The statement asks whether every closed convex C^2 surface in Euclidean 3-space has at least two umbilic points. Before the window: analytic-case proofs by Hamburger (1940-41), Bol (1944), Titus (1973) and Ivanov (2002), with gaps alleged by Klotz (1959) and Scherbel (1993), so the analytic chain itself is disputed; Guilfoyle and Klingenberg posted a proof for C^{3+alpha} strictly convex surfaces in 2008 (v4 Oct 2024), with three parts published 2019-2024, and their own text says the C^2 conjecture is not what they prove; their 2012 index bound (current v3, Mar 2026: index less than two for C^{3+alpha}) also gives the C^{3+alpha} case. In-window: Guckenheimer (Feb 2024) gives a simpler argument for the analytic case only, and does not discuss the 2008 proof; Guilfoyle and Klingenberg's 2025 survey restates the 2008 proof as published, with no new Euclidean result; Ando and Umehara (Dec 2025) claimed the C^2 case and withdrew after finding a gap, saying the manuscript should not be cited; Levent Alpöge announced on 19 Aug 2026 an explicit C^infinity counterexample with one umbilic of index 2. The announcement is recorded from secondary sources: the X post returned HTTP 402 and no write-up was located. Wikipedia says it was checked with John-Paul Smith and Anthropic's Claude; the formalisation page reproduces the formula and says the write-up is not public at the time of writing; a Chinese press report of 21 Aug 2026 says a PDF was made public, with no link. The Lean formalisation is in two draft PRs in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (#5066, #5070), authored by a GitHub user Paul-Lez, with no reviews; the PR says it was developed with Codex and parallel proof-review agents, which I treat as formalisation rather than the mathematics. VibeMathed, which tracks the claim, records 'Candidate (review pending)' and 'No independent mathematician has checked this yet' as of its last audit (21 Aug 2026). Close call: whether the Alpöge event settles the problem depends on whether its construction holds. If it does, the 2008 and 2026 Guilfoyle-Klingenberg results are false for smooth surfaces, which this record cannot resolve. AI: the only system named for the Alpöge result is Claude, credited in secondary sources with checking the construction; whether it contributed to finding the example is not stated in any source I could open. I did not find any AI involvement in the other events. The separate July 2026 Jacobian conjecture claim credited to Claude Fable 5 is a different problem and is not recorded here.
competing_reading: Reading the Alpöge construction as correct: it is explicit, the Lean audit reports no sorry and no declared axioms, and a smooth counterexample is exactly what the universal statement excludes; on that reading the 2008 Guilfoyle-Klingenberg theorem for C^{3+alpha} and their 2026 index bound are false for smooth surfaces, and the problem is refuted in its smooth form. Reading the event as not yet a resolution: no mathematician reading is recorded; the human write-up was not located; the formalisation is an unmerged draft whose author wrote 'please ignore' and whose audit says 'read, not compiled'; the claim is secondhand throughout. A published-journal record exists for Guilfoyle-Klingenberg's parts and none for the Alpöge claim. Both readings are supported by the record; the choice belongs to the judging pass.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The Alpöge write-up or the X post text; the Chinese report says a PDF was made public, but no link was found. (2) Merge and compilation of formal-conjectures PR #5070, with the statement audited against IsConvexSphereOfClass. (3) An independent computation of the umbilics and indices of g_2, or a referee report. (4) A response from Guilfoyle and Klingenberg, or a withdrawal or erratum for arXiv:0808.0851 v4 or arXiv:1207.5994 v3. (5) For the AI question: Alpöge's own account of whether Claude proposed the seed f or the family g_k, or only checked it.
